question: Which statement best describes Create a list?
options: `.map()` calls a function for each item and returns a new array of transformed results. For example, map product records to the labels shown in a dropdown. Use it when each input should produce one output. Avoid map for side effects when a loop communicates the intent more clearly. Map creates a new outer array, but object items inside are still references. Avoid mutating those objects if other code shares them. Map is like passing every item through the same label maker.

An array stores an ordered list of values in square brackets, such as `["tea", "bread"]`. It is useful when items belong together and their position matters. A shopping list is a familiar example. Arrays can contain objects too, such as a list of product records returned by an API. Arrays preserve item order and can grow or shrink. Use an array when position or iteration matters, and use an object when values are better identified by names.

Indexes start at zero, so `items[0]` reads the first item. The last index is `items.length - 1`; an empty array has no last item. Check the length before reading a calculated position. This prevents `undefined` values from appearing when a list has no matching records. An index can be outside the current bounds after a list changes. Check the array’s length before reading a computed position. An array index is like a seat number that starts at zero.

`.length` gives the number of items, not the last index. For a three-item array, length is 3 and the final index is 2. Use it to check whether a collection is empty or control a loop. Do not assume a list always contains at least one item. Length updates when items are added or removed. A loop should compare its index against the current length and avoid modifying the collection unexpectedly. Array length counts the seats, while the last seat number is one less.
